Yields on Nigerian Treasury bills rose across all maturities at Wednesday’s primary market auction, with the 364-day instrument recording the steepest increase as investors demanded higher returns for lending to the Federal Government. Results of the November 25, 2026 auction showed that the stop rates on the 91-day, 182-day and 364-day bills increased to 16.00 per cent, 16.14 per cent and 16.60 per cent, respectively. The latest adjustments represent increases from 15.40 per cent, 15.79 per cent and 15.89 per cent recorded at the preceding auction. The repricing occurred despite the Central Bank of Nigeria’s decision to retain its benchmark Monetary Policy Rate at 23 per cent at its November Monetary Policy Committee meeting. Data from the auction showed that investors submitted bids worth N882.77bn against the N600bn offered, representing a subscription rate of 147.1 per cent. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. The bulk of investor demand was concentrated in the one-year instrument, highlighting the preference for longer-dated government securities despite the higher returns required by investors. The 364-day T-bill attracted N794.16bn in subscriptions, accounting for approximately 90 per cent of total bids. Against an initial offer of N400bn, the CBN allotted N625.08bn at a stop rate of 16.60 per cent, compared with 15.89 per cent at the previous auction. Borrowing Nigerians can believe in T-bill yield climbs to 17.82% on sell-off UPDATED: CBN retains interest rate at 23%, warns of election spending risks This represented a 71-basis-point increase, making the one-year instrument the most aggressively repriced security at the auction. The shorter maturities attracted considerably less interest. The 182-day bill received subscriptions of N51.06bn, all of which were allotted, while the 91-day instrument attracted N37.54bn in bids, with N37.14bn accepted. The results indicate that investors were more willing to commit funds for longer periods, potentially seeking to lock in higher returns amid uncertainty over interest rates, inflation and the naira’s direction. Cowry Asset Management Limited, in its assessment of the auction, said yields increased across the maturity spectrum, with the largest adjustment occurring at the one-year end. The investment firm noted that the upward-sloping yield structure reflected investors’ preference for higher compensation for committing funds over longer periods. It also observed that the 364-day instrument dominated subscriptions, while demand for the shorter-term bills remained below their respective offer levels. The latest auction suggests that the government’s domestic borrowing costs remain sensitive to investor return expectations, even as the CBN maintains its benchmark interest rate. The increase in T-bill yields could also raise the cost of short-term government borrowing and influence returns available on other naira-denominated investment instruments. Odinaka Anudu
